title: Make.com Advanced: Custom Functions, Error Routes, and Advanced Modules
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Make.com Advanced: Custom Functions, Error Routes, and Advanced Modules ##### The scenario that stopped at record 847 A nightly job pushed 3,000 product records from a PIM system to a marketplace API. It ran fine for months. Then one product had a description containing an unescaped control character, the API returned `400 Bad Request`, and the scenario halted. Records 1–846 had been pushed. Records 848–3,000 had not. Nobody knew which, because the operator's only signal was an email saying "scenario failed." The rerun pushed all 3,000 again, creating 846 duplicates on the marketplace. One malformed description cost a day of cleanup. The fix is a single error handler with an **Ignore** directive on that module, plus an idempotent write — perhaps ten minutes of work, if you know the mechanism exists. Make's error-handling system is its most underused capability, and its function language is what collapses long module chains into single expressions. Together they are the difference between scenarios that work and scenarios that survive. ##### IML: Make's expression language Every mapping field in Make accepts **IML (Integromat Markup Language)** expressions — `{{...}}` containing functions, operators and references. Because they evaluate *inside* an existing module, they cost **zero additional operations**. Every transformation you push into an expression instead of a Tools module is a direct saving. The function families worth knowing well: ```javascript // Strings {{ trim(upper(1.customer.country)) }} {{ substring(1.description; 0; 200) }} {{ replace(1.phone; "/[^0-9]/g"; "") }} // regex replace {{ split(1.tags; ",") }} {{ join(map(1.items; "sku"); ", ") }} // Numbers and money {{ round(sum(map(1.items; "price")) * 1.18; 2) }} {{ formatNumber(1.total; 2; "."; ",") }} {{ parseNumber(replace(1.raw_price; "/[^0-9.]/g"; ""); ".") }} // Dates — always pass a timezone explicitly {{ formatDate(1.created; "YYYY-MM-DD"; "Asia/Kolkata") }} {{ addDays(now; 7) }} {{ parseDate(1.date_text; "DD/MM/YYYY"; "Asia/Kolkata") }} // Arrays — the high-value ones {{ map(1.items; "sku") }} // pluck a field {{ filter(1.items; "status"; "confirmed") }} // subset {{ sum(map(filter(1.items; "status"; "confirmed"); "amount")) }} {{ length(1.items) }} {{ first(sort(1.items; "created")) }} {{ distinct(map(1.items; "category")) }} {{ flatten(1.grouped) }} // Conditionals and null handling {{ if(1.total > 5000; "enterprise"; "standard") }} {{ ifempty(1.company; "Unknown") }} {{ switch(1.status; "new"; "🆕"; "paid"; "✅"; "❓") }} ``` Two behaviours worth internalizing. `ifempty()` treats empty strings, nulls and absent values uniformly, which is usually what you want for defaults. And **`get()` is your guard against missing nested keys** — `{{ get(1.customer.address; "city") }}` returns empty rather than erroring when `address` is null, which prevents a whole class of runtime failures. The `map(filter(...))` composition deserves emphasis: computing a filtered sum inline replaces an Iterator, a Filter, and a Numeric Aggregator — three modules and a bundle multiplication, reduced to one expression evaluated for free. ##### Error handlers and the five directives Right-click any module → **Add error handler**, and you get a separate route that executes when that module throws. What you attach to that route determines the scenario's behaviour, and Make gives you five directives with genuinely different semantics. **Resume** — substitute a value and continue as though the module succeeded. The error route computes a fallback output, and downstream modules receive it. *Use when the step is optional enrichment.* A geocoding lookup fails → Resume with `{lat: null, lng: null, geocode_status: "failed"}` and carry on. The record still gets saved. **Ignore** — discard this bundle and continue with the next. The rest of the route does not run for this item. *Use for per-record data problems in a batch.* This is the fix for the opening story: one malformed product is skipped and logged, and the other 2,999 process normally. **Break** — park the failed bundle in the **incomplete executions** queue and continue the scenario. Make can then retry it automatically on a schedule you configure (retry interval and attempt count), or you can retry it manually from the UI. *Use for transient failures against an external service.* This is Make's dead-letter queue and its most valuable directive. **Commit** — stop the scenario immediately but keep everything already done. No rollback. *Use when partial completion is acceptable and continuing would compound the problem* — for example, you have detected the API is rate-limiting you and want to stop cleanly rather than burn operations. **Rollback** — stop the scenario and roll back transactional operations where the modules support it (database transactions, some app modules). *Use when partial completion is worse than nothing* — a multi-step financial posting that must be all-or-nothing. ```mermaid flowchart TD M[HTTP: push product] -.error handler.-> E{Classify error} E -->|429 / 5xx transient| B[Break
→ incomplete executions
auto-retry in 15 min] E -->|400 / 422 bad record| I[Ignore
→ log to failures sheet
continue next bundle] E -->|optional enrichment| R[Resume
→ default values
flag for later] E -->|rate limit detected| C[Commit
→ stop cleanly, alert] E -->|financial multi-step| RB[Rollback
→ undo, alert] ``` Two configuration details that matter in production. **Enable "Allow storing of Incomplete Executions"** in scenario settings, or Break has nowhere to park failures. And **error handlers can contain full routes** — log to a sheet, post to Slack, *then* apply the directive — so the directive is the last module in the handler, not the only one. ##### The HTTP module and Make's own API The **HTTP → Make a request** module makes any REST API reachable, exactly as Custom Request does in Zapier. Key settings: method, URL, headers, query string, body type (Raw with `application/json` for most APIs), and — importantly — **"Evaluate all states as errors"**, which controls whether a 4xx throws or returns as data. That checkbox is a design decision. Leaving it *off* means a 404 returns as a normal bundle with `statusCode: 404`, letting you branch on the status with a router rather than an error handler. That is often cleaner for expected non-2xx responses, such as a lookup that legitimately may not find anything. Other useful HTTP options: **Parse response** (auto-JSON), **Timeout** (raise it for slow endpoints, but stay under the scenario limit), and the **OAuth 2.0 request** variant, which handles token refresh for APIs Make has no app for. Separately, the **Make API** module lets scenarios manage Make itself — list scenarios, read execution logs, activate or deactivate scenarios, trigger another scenario. This enables genuinely useful meta-automation: a monitoring scenario that queries execution history, computes a success rate, and alerts when it drops. ##### Advanced arrays and scenario optimization Iterators and aggregators are covered ground; the advanced concerns are about **cost** and **bundle discipline**. Make bills per module execution per bundle. The multiplication is where scenarios get expensive: ```text BEFORE ops/run Webhook 1 Iterator (300 items) 1 Tools: Set variable ×300 300 Tools: Text aggregator ×300 300 HTTP: POST per item ×300 300 Sheets: Add row ×300 300 ----- 1,202 AFTER Webhook 1 Filter on the route (free) — drops 240 items 0 Iterator (60 items remain) 1 HTTP: POST per item ×60 60 Array aggregator → single batch 1 Sheets: Bulk add rows 1 ----- 64 (-95%) ``` The five levers, in order of impact: 1. **Filter on routes before iterating.** Route filters cost nothing and prevent the multiplication entirely. 2. **Use batch endpoints.** One HTTP call with 100 records beats 100 calls — fewer operations, faster, and easier on rate limits. 3. **Do transformations in IML inside an existing module** rather than adding Tools modules. 4. **Set a bundle limit** on triggers (`Maximum number of returned bundles`) so a backlog does not process 5,000 items in one run and time out. 5. **Aggregate before writing.** One bulk row insert instead of 300 individual ones. Also worth knowing: **Data structures** (defined schemas for webhooks and JSON parsing) give you reliable field mapping instead of guessing, and scenario **Auto-commit / sequential processing** settings control whether bundles process independently or as a unit. ##### A resilient bulk-processing pattern Putting the pieces together for the mini project's shape: ```text 1 Trigger / HTTP: fetch batch (bundle limit 500) 2 Route filter: skip already-processed (free — checks a data store flag) 3 Iterator: split the array 4 IML transform inline in the next module (no Tools module) 5 HTTP: POST item ├─ error handler → Router │ ├─ statusCode in 429,500,502,503 → log + BREAK (auto-retry) │ ├─ statusCode in 400,422 → log + IGNORE (skip poison record) │ └─ otherwise → alert + COMMIT 6 Data store: mark item processed (idempotency) 7 Array aggregator: collect results 8 Sheets: bulk write summary + failure list ``` Note that Break and Ignore land on the *same* module with different classifications — the router inside the error handler is what distinguishes transient from permanent, exactly as retry logic does in code. ##### Common pitfalls - **No error handlers**, so one bad record halts the batch mid-way. - **Incomplete executions disabled**, making Break silently useless. - **Break on a permanent 400**, retrying forever something that will never succeed. - **Ignore on a transient 503**, silently dropping records that would have succeeded. - **Rollback assumed to undo API calls** — it only rolls back modules that support transactions. You cannot un-send an email. - **Iterating before filtering**, multiplying operations by 5×. - **Missing timezone in `formatDate`**, producing dates shifted by 5.5 hours. - **Deep field access without `get()`**, erroring on a null parent. - **No bundle limit** on a trigger, so a backlog produces a timeout. - **Error handlers that only apply a directive** without logging, leaving no trace of what was skipped. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: build a scenario using **advanced IML functions** to transform data, attach an **error handler with a Resume directive** to a flaky module, and use the **HTTP module** to call an API with no native app. Force the failure deliberately — point the flaky module at an invalid endpoint — and confirm the scenario continues with your fallback values rather than halting. The mini project is the resilient bulk processor: iterate a large array, transform with IML, call an external API via HTTP with **Break for transient failures with retry** and **Ignore for known-skippable errors**, aggregate results, log failures, and **optimize for minimal operations**. Record the operation count before and after optimization — that percentage is the most persuasive line in your write-up, and it demonstrates the cost reasoning that marks an intermediate practitioner. For the assignment, explain **each of the five directives** with a scenario where it is correct, and describe **two ways to reduce operation cost**. For the directives, the distinguishing question is always: *is this record recoverable, skippable, or fatal?* For cost, filter-before-iterate and inline-IML-instead-of-Tools-modules are the two with the largest measured impact. ##### Key takeaways - IML expressions evaluate inside existing modules at zero operation cost — pushing transformations into them is the cheapest optimization available. - Use `get()` for safe nested access, `ifempty()` for defaults, and `map(filter(...))` to replace whole iterate-filter-aggregate chains. - The five error directives are distinct tools: Resume for optional steps, Ignore for poison records, Break for transient failures with retry, Commit for clean early stops, Rollback for all-or-nothing transactions. - Classify errors inside the handler with a router so transient and permanent failures get different directives — and always log before applying one. - Cut operations by filtering on routes before iterating, batching API calls, aggregating before writes, and setting trigger bundle limits.
